book: The Kalpa Sutra — Lives of the Tirthankaras

1: In that period, in that age, the Venerable Ascetic Mahavira descended from the upper heavens, where he had lived for twenty Sagaropamas, into the womb of the lady Trishala, of the house of the Jnatrikas. And the night of his descent the lady saw fourteen great dreams: a white elephant, a white bull, a lion, the Goddess of Wealth, and ten more — and the interpreters said: A Tirthankara, a maker of the ford across the river of the world, is come.

And when he was born, the gods hailed him with the thirty-two marks of a great man, and the eighty-three lesser signs — for he who comes to show the way is known before he speaks, and his body is a scripture that those who can read bodies can read.
2: In the first month of the rainy season, in the second fortnight, on the tenth day of the dark half of Ashadha, in the Muhurta called Vigaya, in the spot called the park of the Jnatrikas — the Venerable One, after fasting two and a half days without drinking water, tore out his hair in five handfuls, and went forth to the homeless state. And the gods came to witness it, and the witness of the gods is written: thus goes the one who goes all the way.

For more than twelve years he wandered, neglecting his body, practising the highest austerity, meditating by day and by night. In the cold season he meditated in the shade; in the heat, in the sun. He endured the rude and hard words of men, and the bites of the flies, and the silence of the forest — and through all of it he kept the vow of ahimsa as a mother keeps her child: with both arms, and without sleep.
3: During the thirteenth year, in the second month of summer, in the fourth fortnight, in the bright fortnight of Vaishakha, on its tenth day, when the moon was in conjunction with the asterism Uttarashadha, outside the town of Jrimbhikagrama, on the northern bank of the river Rjupalika, not far from an old temple, on a couch of straw — with knees bent and held with his hands, exposed to the sun — he reached the state of perfect knowledge. And the knowledge was called kevala, the alone, because nothing in the three worlds was outside it.

And the Venerable One taught: The living world is fivefold — the earth-bodied, the water-bodied, the fire-bodied, the wind-bodied, and the plants — and the moving beings besides. All of them desire life and abhor death, and all of them feel pain, and he who knows this is the sage, and his teaching is one word long, and the word is ahimsa: harm no one — and the word is long enough for a whole life, and it has filled the lives of the best of us.
